sp: COMMITTEE ON WOMEN AND GENDER EQUITY
p: Thank you. We will now move into the Discussion of Resolutions, beginning with our Public Advocate, Jumaane Williams.

Thank you very much. My objective this third time of reading these remarks is to try to get through it without so many pauses, but I do want to acknowledge Emma O'Connell and Jason Kaplan from the Tourette Syndrome Association, who are with us today. So there are several people in the audience with Tourette's Syndrome. And just to let everyone know, that can get interesting. So I just want folks to know. Good afternoon, again. My name is Jumaane Williams; I'm the Public Advocate of the city of New York. I want to thank Speaker Menin, Chair Hanif, and the Members of the Committee and the Council for holding this vote. I’d like to thank the advocates in the audience for attending today's Stated Meeting.

The CDC estimates that about 1.4 million people in the US have Tourette's Syndrome or a persistent tic disorder. I am one of those people, and I am believed to be the first person with Tourette's in the country to be elected to public office. People with Tourette's experience tics, involuntary, sudden, brief, intermittent, repetitive movements or noises. It can significantly impact a person's day-to-day, and can either be temporary or something a person lives with for the rest of their life. People with Tourette's are also more likely to have other comorbid disabilities, such as learning disabilities, autism, and depression. I myself have also been diagnosed with ADHD. While Tourette's Syndrome itself can make day-to-day life difficult, so too does a lack of awareness about it. Many people have never heard of Tourette's or have heard misinformation, and may react negatively, even violently, to a person's tics. I myself lived with Tourette's for a time, not knowing what it was. And in fact, I first

learned about Tourette's from a 20/20 Special, not from a doctor. Tourette's is too often viewed as a moral failing, as if a person is refusing to stop the tics rather than being unable to. This is especially so when a tic is obscene language or a slur called Coprolalia, something I have struggled with. Stigma and discrimination can make getting and keeping a job more difficult or lead to increased contact with the criminal legal system. Many people with Tourette's retreat from public life, isolating themselves from other people due to shame or fear, and may avoid seeking treatment. Recently, at the BAFTA Awards, John Davidson, an activist who educates people about Tourette's Syndrome, shouted out the N word as two Black actors were presenting awards, setting off a firestorm of media attention and outrage. Tics that include offensive language and slurs can cause real hurt, even if the person saying it not only does not intend harm, but is deeply regretful and embarrassed by it.

As a Black man who also tics the N word, I know no matter the reason, that word has power and does real damage. And we can't minimize it. I think we can recognize that even an involuntary impact devoid of intent can't be ignored. Too often, the burden of empathy is placed primarily on the Black community. At the same time, to the importance of this Resolution, we also have to make space for compassion and grace for the person with Tourette's and take this opportunity to educate people about the disability. The situation at the BAFTAs never should have happened, but it did, so let's learn from it. At that moment, BAFTA had a responsibility to prepare the attendees for the possibility that they may have had this language directed at them. They also had the ability not to hear it. Now we have an opportunity to inform people more broadly. Education and awareness have proven to be effective in combating stigma against disabilities and other disorders. Today, we're voting on a resolution I introduced declaring May 15th through June 15th as Tourette’s Syndrome Awareness Month and

June 7th as Tourette's Syndrome Awareness Day in New York City. Knowing people with a disability reduces stigma, underscoring the need for raising awareness, representation, and open dialogue about Tourette's and other tic disorders. I hope that young people living with tic disorders can see their own potential in me. And I hope everyone will join me in celebrating this newly recognized month and day. I was the first elected official in the country known to have Tourette's Syndrome, and I'm proud to say I am no longer the only one. And I want young people like me out there to know that your condition is a part of you, but you are not defined by it. And it doesn't have to limit what you do, only change how you do it. And by more broadly recognizing Tourette's Syndrome Awareness Month, I hope we can reach others with that message. I want to thank my staff, Gwen Saffran, Senior Policy and Legislative Associate; Veronica Aveis, Deputy Public Advocate for Policy; Rosie Mendez, Director of Policy and Legislation; Elizabeth

Kennedy, Deputy Public Advocate for Education and Opportunity; and Lupe Hernandez, Community Organizer. I would also like to thank the Tourette Association of America for its work on this resolution. And I want to shout out to Justin Farmer from Connecticut, who ran for office and won after he saw me. That was an amazing moment of pride. I also want to thank Cameron (phonetic) Jackson, whose grandmother was in a committee hearing earlier, who stopped me at an event to tell me he had Tourette’s Syndrome. I was happy to be able to invite him to my office. I am happy to bring him here to City Hall as well. I have never hidden my Tourette’s Syndrome, and I never plan to. I never leaned into it intentionally, but I am trying to do that more. I am also trying to honor the experience of my younger self. So, I thank you all for voting for this, and for helping me live to be who you needed when you were younger. Thank you.
Thank you, Mr. Public Advocate. (APPLAUSE)
Wow. Council Member Schulman?

Thank you, Majority Leader. Today's vaccine package is very timely. I just learned it's World Immunization Week. As part of today's package, I am proud to sponsor three resolutions being voted on today, each one a direct response to the growing threats to vaccine access and public health in our city and state. None of this would be possible without the Speaker's commitment to making New York City a leader on public health. The first Resolution, 273-A, calls on New York State to authorize dentists to administer vaccines. Dentists were on the front lines of our COVID response. They showed up, they were qualified, and they saved lives. It's time to make that permanent. Every additional access point means more New Yorkers are protected. The second Resolution, 425, calls on New York State to require vaccine policy to be grounded in the recommendations of reputable nationally and internationally recognized healthcare organizations, not solely on a CDC, which has become increasingly

politicized. The federal government is eroding public trust in vaccines and putting lives at risk. New York will not follow them down that path. And finally, Preconsidered Resolution 448 calls on New York State to require insurers to fully reimburse pediatric practices for the cost of providing vaccines. Pediatric offices are the backbone of our childhood immunization system, and we must make sure they can afford to stay there. (TIMER) When Washington steps back, the City Council steps up. Thank you.

The ayes have it. We will now move into General Discussion, first beginning with Council Member Hanks, followed by Council Member Narcisse.

Thank you, Majority Leader. First, I want to say how proud I am to support our Public Advocates’ resolutions on Tourette's Syndrome awareness. Thank you for your advocacy. I know what it's like. I raised the stepdaughter for 20 years with Tourette's, and what you said was absolutely moving, and thank you very much. Heart disease remains one of the leading causes of death in New York City and across New York State. It affects families in every borough, every community in every neighborhood. Reso 442 calls on New York State to require insurance coverage for coronary artery calcium testing so that more New Yorkers can benefit from this important preventative tool. It is a common-sense step that can help save lives, reduce long-term healthcare costs, and give families a chance to act before a medical emergency occurs. Coronary artery calcium testing is a simple,

non-invasive screening tool that can help identify plaque buildup in arteries and give patients and doctors a clearer picture of heart disease risk. For many people, it could be the early warning that leads to lifestyle changes, medication, further testing, and ultimately life-saving care. For too many New Yorkers, the test is out of reach because it's not covered by insurance. That means prevention becomes a question of whether someone can afford to pay out of pocket. And that is not how our healthcare system should work. Not long ago, my partner's life was changed because of early detection through coronary artery calcium testing. It revealed a serious risk that would never have been known otherwise, and he had no warning signs or anything that would tell us something was wrong. No family should have to learn too late that there was a tool available that could have helped them detect a problem earlier. I call on my colleagues to support this resolution. Thank you, Mr. Majority Leader.
Council Member Narcisse, followed by Council Member Wong.

Thank you, Majority Leader, and thank you, Public Advocate, for this bill, which is needed in our city so we can be sensitive to each other and understand the disease process, whatever we're going through. So thank you for sharing. I'm proud to introduce two bills, and thank you to Speaker Menin. These bills are very important. The first one is the dog waste. I know for some it's not a big deal. This is a quality-of-life issue every day. New Yorkers know too well that when you walk out your front door, you have to dodge the sidewalk from stepping on poops all over. Your kids are standing on them in the park. There are 600,000 dogs in the city, 3-11 complaints are up to 81%, and sanitation issues have issued just two summonses in all of 2025. The law exists, but nobody is being held to it. This bill puts up signs where the problem is worse on the park sidewalks. Neighborhoods are calling 3-11 over and over to get relief. That's what we are looking for. So the rules can apply to all people, and we can end this. This is happening too

often. So I'm asking my colleagues to look into this and support me. I'm also introducing the Homeowner Stability and Protection Act today, Intro 879. Local Law 18 was supposed to lower costs and expand housing. But years later, rents are still skyrocketing, and the vacancy rate has not budged. What does this do? It takes away the ability of homeowners to earn income from their own homes. In my district and in working-class neighborhoods across the city, homeowners are losing their homes. Deed thefts have nearly tripled since 2023. We have seen over 1,800 foreclosures across the 10 majority Black communities around the city. This is too much. The seniors are losing their homes. It is time for us to step up. This bill (TIMER) lets homeowners have their home while they're traveling, raising the guest cap from two to four, so a family... (CROSS-TALK)
Please wrap up, Council Member... (CROSS-TALK)
can actually stay together. This is important, and thank you, Majority Leader. So let's look into it.
Council Member Wong, followed by Council Member Hankerson.

Thank you, Majority Leader. Today, I am introducing six pieces of legislation that will improve the safety, equity, and quality of life in the city. My first focus is on improving community awareness of their schools. To accomplish this, Intro 885 would require the Department of Education to create an online portal to facilitate the comparison of funding and spending across schools. Two of my other bills would increase the safety of our neighborhoods. Intro 889 would prohibit the parking of commercial vehicles owned or operated by gas or oil heat suppliers between the hours of 9:00 P.M. and 5:00 A.M., and Intro 887 would make it an immediate hazardous violation to sell beverages without a valid place of assembly certificate of operation. Additionally, two of the bills would greatly increase our knowledge of what is happening behind the scenes. Intro 886 would require the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene to publicly

issue monthly reports on animal shelters that are under contract with the City of New York. Intro 888 would require the Department of Health to report how many times city agencies and hospitals submit referrals for individuals to assisted outpatient treatment programs. My final bill, Intro 890, would improve the City's relationship with the environment and save us money by creating a pilot program to study increasing the minimum percentage of reclaimed asphalt pavement. All of these bills have different focuses, but they are common-sense measures that will meaningfully improve the safety and quality of life of all New Yorkers. Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member. I would also like to recognize that former council members have joined us, now State Legislators, Erik Bottcher, our senator, and Keith Powers from the Assembly. (APPLAUSE)
Council Member Hankerson, followed by Council Member Brooks-Powers.
Thank you, Majority Leader. I just want to take a moment to recognize the young people from the Learning to Work program who have joined us in the balcony today for nearly 20... (APPLAUSE)

Absolutely... For nearly 20 years, Learning to Work has kept young people on track to graduate. It serves more than 16,000 students across the city. These are students who fell behind and are working to catch up. My little brother was one of them. This program provided the support, positivity, and mentorship he needed. But he isn't the only one. Thousands of young people across the city of New York have benefited from this program. If we are serious about investing in our youth, we must keep them engaged with programs that work. If we are serious about decreasing unemployment, we must prepare them for work. If we are serious about the economy, we must be intentional about valuing their voices and harnessing their creativity.

Students in this program have counselors who stay with them. They recover credits and move toward a diploma. They step into paid internships and build real work experience—students in this program graduate at higher rates. Interns graduate at rates near 97% from the program. Right now, this program is not guaranteed to continue at full strength. Support has shifted to short-term fixes that create instability. That instability reaches students and staff. If this program shrinks, thousands of young people lose support. More students will leave school without a diploma. We will feel that in our workforce and in our communities. If we are serious about decreasing youth crime, we must protect what keeps young people on track. If we are serious about decreasing unemployment, we should protect what they do for work. If we are serious about the economy, we protect the systems that build it. Thank you to the Learning to Work students who are here with us today.
Thank you, Council Member... (APPLAUSE)
Council Member Brooks-Powers, followed by Council Member Brewer.

Thank you. Today, I'm proud to introduce two pieces of legislation aimed at expanding access to affordable homeownership across our city. Homeownership remains one of the most effective tools we have to build generational wealth and stabilize communities. Yet, for too many New Yorkers, especially working families, that pathway remains out of reach. The first bill I'm introducing, Intro 862, which strengthened the city's Home First Down Payment Assistance Program by requiring HPD to assist at least 600 first-time home buyers each year. This program provides up to $100,000 in support for down payments and closing costs, but it is currently underutilized. In fiscal year 2025, only 126 households were assisted. While the agency is working to scale up to 300 loans annually, this bill works to expand affordable homeownership opportunities by doubling that number to 600 households per year. The second bill, Intro 861, focuses on awareness and access. It would require HPD to conduct

a targeted outreach campaign to inform New York residents about the Section 8 Home Ownership Program, which allows eligible families to use their vouchers towards purchasing a home. Shout out to my Assembly member, Khaleel Anderson, on this one. Together, these bills can move us closer to realizing the dream of home ownership for thousands more New Yorkers. Additionally, I'm introducing Resolution 439 in support of state legislation restoring 20-year service retirement for uniform correction officers and sanitation workers. At a time when our correctional system is facing significant staffing challenges, restoring parity and benefits is a critical step towards improving conditions for both staff and those in custody. (TIMER) I look forward to working with my colleagues to advance these efforts. Thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Brewer, followed by Council Member Morano.

Thank you. I just want to say we need an exterminator because we had a water bug over here,

and I know what water bugs look like because I’ve got them in my house. I just want to let you know. So Intro 859 (BACKGROUND NOISE)... Intro 859, twice a year, the City Council...
Keep it down, let the council member speak, thank you.

I brought up the problem. Twice a year, the City Council honors New Yorkers with street co-namings. I think many of us have done this, mostly people we know. For instance, I just honored salsa pianist Larry Harlow on West 86th Street. To familiarize more New Yorkers with those who came before us, the Council passed my Local Law 104 in 2023, and DORIS, which is the records, created a searchable map. In 2002 and 2003, Local Laws named 400+ streets for first responders killed on 9/11, but many of those streets lacked biographical information. Under the guidance of Commissioner Pauline O'Toole of DORIS, her staff compiled the stories of these individuals lost on that terrible

day and found them all. Introduction 859 allows DORIS to update the map accordingly. Introduction 860 authorized HPD and the Fire Department to inspect buildings for required physical street numbers during their routine inspections of buildings. For over 100 years, all buildings in New York City must display their street numbers, so first responders don't lose critical time to help people in need. And yet compliance has been a problem. An article in the New York Times from 1929 noted the lack of building numbers and how it impacted delivery people and telegraph messengers. I passed Local Law 26 and 2017 with Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, if he remembers, and the fire department supports an increase in fines. Intro 860 would empower HPD and the fire department to respond to 3-11 complaints and also add (TIMER) street numbers to their regular inspections. If you ever wander around and can't find a street number, now you'll be able to find it. Thank you very much.

Thank you.

Council Member Maloney, followed by Council Member Morano.
Thank you, Majority Leader. Today...
Sit down, please. Sit down.

Today, I'm introducing three pieces of legislation and a resolution focused on supporting small businesses and keeping our streets safe. The first is Introduction 197, which supports the legacy businesses that have shaped the character of our communities, such as the corner bakery, the family hardware store, or your local diner. This bill would establish a legacy business registry to formally recognize those legacy businesses that have operated for 20+ years, and it would create a preservation fund that would provide grants to those businesses and to property owners who commit to keeping them in place. The second is a resolution that calls on Albany to pass legislation allowing mobile barber shops. I want to thank Assembly Member Jordan Wright,

who is championing that bill in Albany, for being here. Not everyone can go to a barber shop. Seniors and people with disabilities deserve access to professional services just like everyone else, and mobile barber shops meet people where they are, support small business entrepreneurship, and fill a gap in our communities. Third is Introduction 372, which makes government work better and faster. The legislation would require every city agency that issues permits to publish clear timelines so applicants know what to expect. It provides real-time tracking so that they can follow their application every step of the way, and establishes accountability measures to make sure agencies actually meet the timelines that they set. And lastly, Intro 1312 to address a safety issue that has become impossible to ignore, E-bikes going too fast on our streets and on our sidewalks. This legislation would enshrine the speed limit for electric-assist bicycles at 15 mph in City law, and I look forward to working with my colleagues to pass this. Thank you.
Council Member Morano, followed by Council Member Pierina Sanchez.

Thank you. Colleagues, before we leave today, I just want to say a word about what happened in Washington last Saturday. Thank God the president is safe. Thank goodness there were no fatalities. And thank God for the men and women in law enforcement who acted in seconds when it mattered most. But let's be honest with ourselves. This was the third time a president has had to contend with something like this in the last 2-and-a-half years. And that means something is really wrong. And I don't say that to point fingers. I say it because I think the responsibility falls on us, the people in this room, to set a different tone. We argue, we disagree, sometimes loudly, sometimes on television, sometimes on the radio. But the people that we disagree with are not enemies to be destroyed. Their colleagues, their neighbors. In some cases, they've become friends. For instance, Council Member Ossé and I did a video recently on something about as controversial as it gets, changing the clocks. I caught a little heat for it. I'm sure he did too. But you know what people saw? Two members who don't agree on everything—most days, we don't agree on anything—

are actually working together on something. And after what we just witnessed, I am more committed than ever to that approach. I think the more we disagree, the more important it is that we work together because the public needs to see that it's still possible. I always try to have a Democratic prime sponsor on my bills unless the idea is truly crazy, which, assure you, today's bill with Council Member Wong is not. And I think that's what the Common Sense Caucus is all about. And it's something I'm proud to be a part of. We can debate hard without dehumanizing each other. We can fight for our ideas without fearing for our safety. And if we get that right here, maybe, just maybe, it catches on out there among the public, among a population that may be mentally unstable and in some cases, just waiting to repeat the rhetoric of cable news in order to do something crazy. So I'm more committed than ever to work with the people I disagree with most (TIMER) on as many issues as possible. Thank you.
Council Member Pierina Sanchez, followed by Council Member Mealy.

Thank you, Majority Leader.

Ten. Ten shots were fired outside my office on Monday night. This is the reality in my community—the instability. Here's what else is true— Our median income is about $25,000 per year for a worker who works full-time. Only 16% of our children have access to afterschool programs, and 70% of our families are one income shock away from losing their home. But we're resilient. We're diamonds made in the rough. I grew up here, as have so many others who are fighting each day. When I asked my resilient neighbors what we need the most, the answer was unanimous—a stable home. That's the foundation for stabilizing a community and giving folks the breathing room they need to get ahead in life and be safe. That's why in 2023, this Council passed an expansion to the CityFHEPS program so families don't have to become homeless to get help or languish in a shelter. Because even today, two-thirds of families in shelters are ineligible for a voucher and cannot get out. We expanded FEPS eligibility because homelessness has devastating impacts. Many studies show worse health outcomes, more emergency room

visits, increased intra-family violence, and disruptions in children's education. In New York City, 150,000 students are in shelter; 63% of them are chronically absent. So the cost of inaction is real—42,000 families have been evicted since we passed these bills in 2023—25,000 of those could have been prevented, and it is cheaper. It is cheaper to keep people in their homes, not just because of all of the impacts that I've described, but because shelter, which houses 44,000 households, is costing us $4 billion, whereas we're housing more people with FHEPS today for one-quarter of that price at $1.2 billion. So we gathered today to call on the Mayor to drop his suit. (TIMER) Thank you, Speaker Menin, for your support in keeping vulnerable New Yorkers at the forefront of this negotiation. Thank you.
All right, we have three more to go, and then we will be done soon. Council Member Mealy, followed by Council Member Hanif, then Council Member Zhuang.

Thank you, Madam Speaker, for all the leadership you are showing and

the awareness that you have brought to this city with Denim Day. Today's press conference of Denim Day raised awareness and made it clear that survivors' voices must be heard. Denim Day began after a rape victim's case was overturned due to the claim that tight jeans implied consent. Outraged, people worldwide adopted jeans as a symbol of protest against harmful myths about sexual assault. I want to encourage two organizations today that held their press conference, working in all of our communities: Sisters in Purple and Women Divide. Today was all about everyone advocating to make sure that survivors' voices are never ignored or silenced. And I want to thank my school in my district again. Principal Lena Gates of Dr. Ronald E. McNair/P.S.5 school has been named a 2026 Blue Ribbon Lighthouse School of Excellence for the National Assessment in all nine categories of learning needs. They are doing a big press conference and event today, and I want to thank them all for doing that. And I want to thank Camber (phonetic) and Breevort Senior Center for having their Spades

tournament that happens from 6:00 to 9:00 P.M. And, I thank my team, the Baddies, we won second place. So thank you to the senior centers in all our districts, and make sure our seniors are at the forefront of everything we do in this city. Thank you.
Thank you. Now we have Council Member Hanif, followed by Council Member Zhuang.

Thank you, Majority Leader. With the rain coming down today, things are feeling a little dreary and, honestly, a bit crappy. On my walk to the train this morning, I was greeted by a common sight, a familiar New York hazard, a pile of dog poop on the sidewalk. And as many of you remember, when the winter storm froze our streets earlier this week, it also uncovered a not-so-hidden reality. Far too many New Yorkers are still not picking up after their dogs. That's why today I'm proud to introduce legislation creating a citywide public education campaign to make sure New Yorkers know how to properly dispose of dog waste and understand the real public health risks when they

don't. Being a good neighbor means doing your civic duty. So to all New Yorkers, scoop the poop. Thank you.
Council Member Zhuang?

Thank you, Majority Leader. I want to thank Chair Sanchez for advocating for all New Yorkers. A lot of times, only when we expand the CityFHEPS program are we able to address the homelessness issue in our city, so we don't have to give more money to greedy and corrupt developers to build incentive shelters everywhere in the city. As a mother, I care deeply about education for our city's children, and I know how important it is to be taught how to engage with government. A lot of times, the younger generation doesn't get civic engagement. The Mayor knows how important civic engagement is, too, as shown by his lunch, his morning of organizing Organize NYC. As a result, I'm introducing Resolution 451, calling on the New York State Legislature to pass, and the Governor to sign, A.9298 and a companion bill in the

Senate, which would enact the “Next-Gen Civics Act,” providing hands-on, project-based civic education to students in grades nine through 12. This bill idea is actually an idea from one of our interns from our office. We'd like to encourage more young people to be civically engaged. So it's very important to get our colleagues to sign on to this resolution and support our interns and children in our district, and everywhere in New York City, to know how government works in a way that will encourage and excite them. Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member. I will now call on Speaker Julie Menin to close today’s Stated Meeting.

Great. Thank you. Before I do so, I also want to acknowledge our former colleagues who are here: Assemblymember Keith Powers and State Senator Erik Bottcher. So great to have you back in the chambers. We miss you, but it's great to see you both.
Pass the budget. (LAUGHTER)

Thank you, I heard that. We're counting on you. So the Stated Meeting of April 30th, 2026, is hereby adjourned. Thank you, everyone. [GAVEL]

If you wish to testify, you must see one of the Sergeant at Arms in the back. Please do not approach the dais at any time. Chair, you may begin. CHAIRPERSON FARÍAS: Sergeant, can you bring a gavel? (PAUSE) CHAIRPERSON FARÍAS: [GAVEL] I can officially start. Good morning, everyone. I'm Council Member Amanda Farías, Chair of the Committee on Women and Gender Equity. I'm excited to be joined by the Chair of the Committee on Technology, Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, for today's hearing on protections

, JOINTLY WITH THE COMMITTEE ON TECHNOLOGY 5 against harassment in digital and physical spaces for women and gender expansive people. This morning, we've been joined by Council Members Aldebol, Schulman, and Riley. To start us off, I'm going to turn and read a statement from Council Member Louis. Today, we'll be hearing Resolution Number 99, sponsored by the Council Member, declaring May 28 as Menstrual Hygiene Day in the City of New York.
